newsitem.title: USA: Republican dissent festers amid tax, budget talks.
newsitem.headline: Republican dissent festers amid tax, budget talks.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich urged his Republican supporters Tuesday to focus on major tax and spending bills and put aside differences that brought the party close to civil war over the past two weeks.

But many lawmakers, some firmly on Gingrich's side in the recent turmoil, said they would press for a full airing soon of the issues that brought them to the point where a group of dissidents plotted to oust their speaker the week of July 6, and a high-ranking Republican was forced to quit his leadership post.

Gingrich spokeswoman Christina Martin said the Georgia Republican urged members not to seek a vote on the leadership at Wednesday's regular weekly meeting of all 238 Republican lawmakers. "It is his preference today not to hold a special conference and that we not challenge the leadership in the next conference," she told reporters.

One of Gingrich's backers, Ray LaHood of Illinois, was seen circulating for signatures a resolution that would call a special Republican conference to discuss the aborted coup and the alleged complicity of some in the party's leadership.

Representative Bob Ney of Ohio, a member of the sophomore class which held a meeting on the dissent Tuesday night, felt strongly that party disagreements would have to be cleared if they were to settle down to work on legislation.

"We can't pretend something hasn't happened," he told reporters. However, he said it was not necessary to vote on whether current leaders should stay. "I don't think there will be a vote. People can detect moods...."

Emerging from a lengthy meeting with top Republicans Tuesday night, Gingrich refused to comment on plans to call a special conference, saying only that "I think people agree" with his desire to focus on the budget, not on leadership shakeups.

But Ohio Representative John Boehner, the fourth ranking member of the Republican leadership, told reporters that the tentative plan was to have the regular weekly meeting Wednesday, and probably a special party gathering Thursday.

Many of those dissenters differ sharply with Gingrich over the deals being cut with the Senate and the White House on budget and tax cut bills and have urged that the party move away from the centre line.
Republicans, including Gingrich, however, have said they recognise the need to compromise to the degree necessary to win passage and President Clinton's signatuare.

In an indication of deepening party intrigue, rumours circulated, and were quickly put down, that Republican Whip Tom DeLay of Texas will step down from his leadership position. "He is not resigning," John Feehery said.

Several Republican dissidents pointed to DeLay, the third-ranking Republican in the House, as an active participant in meetings two weeks ago to replace Gingrich with a leader who would take a harder line with the White House on budget and tax negotiations.
At the same time, Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas denied his own complicity in the effort and indicated that another in the party's power structure was involved.
"I apologise for my initial belief that the dissidents were solely responsible for starting this mess," Gingrich deputy Armey said in an emotional letter to his colleagues.

In the two-page letter, Armey affirmed his loyalty to Gingrich and denied publicly for a third time that he had participated in the aborted coup. He said Gingrich was well aware that he did not try to "dump" him.
"Never have I said that I was in favour of any plan to remove the speaker, and no member can truthfully say they ever heard me say that, because I didn't."
"At this point, I couldn't care less whether I'll be speaker, majority leader, or dogcatcher, but I'll be damned if I'll let my name and honour be destroyed," he said.

In his letter, Armey acknowledged he had made mistakes in the past two weeks. He said he attended one meeting in which "what if" scenarios were discussed based on reports of an uprising against Gingrich. He also said he was mistaken to assume no member of the leadership was involved.
